research_rationale: EO 10229 (16 FR 2865, Federal Register of Tuesday, April 3, 1951; signed March 30, 1951; F.R. Doc. 51-4006) has one operative command: under section 204 of the act of June 30, 1932 (47 Stat. 404; 5 U.S.C. 715a) the President exempts Hugh H. Bennett, Chief of the Soil Conservation Service, from compulsory retirement for age under the Civil Service Retirement Act of May 29, 1930, for a stated period. The order fixes its own term, so the first end is the own-terms end date April 30, 1952. Under the 2026-10-21 until-date ruling it is recorded inclusive (the exemption runs through the end of April 30, 1952); the exclusive reading, under which the term ends as April 30 begins, is the alternative. The held Federal Register text confirms identity (number, title, date and document number agree with the census register row). The end is cited to the held Federal Register text of the order itself, a government printed copy (OCR text layer of the official PDF, whose page images were not opened), because the packet registers no own-term record on that text.
savings_reason: The exemption was permission for Bennett to remain in service past the compulsory retirement age during the term; whatever service and pay it allowed before the term ended is accrued. Nothing in the order continues the exemption after the term ends, and the order says nothing about annuity rights, which the Civil Service Retirement Act governs.
earlier_end_check: No held instrument revokes, supersedes, extends or amends EO 10229: the packet's number-citation lookup lists no held order other than the order's own Federal Register page, the later-events catalog search (disposition notes of 6938 catalog records) has no hit for it, and the person-name search finds no other held order naming Hugh H. Bennett. No held record dates Bennett's separation from the Soil Conservation Service, so no event earlier than the stated term is established; if he left earlier, the exemption was unused for the rest of its term but nothing in the order ends it on separation.

research_rationale: EO 10295 (16 FR 10011; signed September 28, 1951) approves a seal of office for the United States Court of Military Appeals: "I hereby approve such seal as the official seal of the United States Court of Military Appeals." The preceding recital describes the design and says the design "accompanies and is hereby made a part of this order". The command is a one-time approval that was complete when the President signed the order; the text has no delayed-effect wording. Under the 2026-10-28 evidence ruling the command is exhausted by performance on September 28, 1951, and the surviving consequence (that the approved design is the Court's official seal) is separated and recorded in savings rather than treated as a command of this order that continues. The dossier's machine own-term leads for this number come from the Court's later rules of practice, which are not this order's terms and are not used.
savings_reason: The approved design remained the Court's official seal as a result of the performed approval. That consequence is separate from the approval command, which is exhausted. Whether any later instrument changed the seal is outside this packet's registered evidence and is not asserted.
conflict_resolutions: {"NO_ORDER_IN_FORCE_ON_1989_01_20":"The 1989 Codification reprints the order's text under a source line that gives its Federal Register and 3 CFR location; it shows the order was published and codified, not that an operative command remained. The order's only operative words are 'I hereby approve such seal as the official seal of the United States Court of Military Appeals', a one-time approval performed on signing, September 28, 1951. The Court's own 1953 rules repeat the seal description and cite this order, which shows the approved design in use as a consequence of the approval; that consequence is recorded in savings and is not treated as a command of this order that continued. The claim does not decide anything about the seal's status after 1953."}
earlier_end_check: The packet's number-citation lookup lists two held texts that cite EO 10295: the 1989 codification note, and the Court's own rules of practice as printed in the Federal Register of June 19, 1953, whose section on the seal repeats the description and gives this order as its source. Both recite the order; neither revokes, supersedes or amends it, and the later-events catalog search has no hit for it. The 1953 rules show the approved design in use as a consequence of the approval, which is recorded in savings and is not a continuing command.
scope_check: One operative clause. The seal's description is part of the order's text but is identification of what is approved, not a second command.
independent_command_check: The order has no appointment, delegation or direction beyond the approval.
savings_check: The approved design remained the Court's official seal as a result of the performed approval. That consequence is separate from the approval command, which is exhausted. Whether any later instrument changed the seal is outside this packet's registered evidence and is not asserted.

The held text of Executive Order No. 8616 is an earlier instrument that this order revokes; it is not a later event.

research_rationale: EO 10417A (17 FR 11187; signed December 6, 1952) closes the executive departments, independent establishments and other agencies in the District of Columbia metropolitan area "all day on Friday, December 26, 1952, the day following Christmas Day," and excuses employees in the metropolitan area and the field service from duty on that day, except those whom agency heads exclude for special public reasons or whose absence would be inconsistent with law. The letter suffix is part of the order number. The command applies to one named day, so it ends with December 26, 1952 by its own terms; the order names the whole day, so the end is the close of that day and the exclusive reading does not arise. The end source is the held Federal Register text of the order itself, which has no separately registered own-term record.
savings_reason: Employees excused from duty on December 26, 1952 were excused for that day, and that excusal is complete; the order continues nothing after that day.
earlier_end_check: The packet's number-citation lookup lists no held order citing EO 10417A other than its own Federal Register page, and the later-events catalog search has no hit for it; no held instrument revokes, supersedes or amends it, so the stated day is the first end.
scope_check: One operative clause: the closing and the excusal both apply to the same day and share the same end. The exceptions for agency heads and for absences inconsistent with law narrow the clause but do not extend it.
independent_command_check: The order has no appointment, delegation or other command separate from the one-day closing and excusal.
savings_check: Employees excused from duty on December 26, 1952 were excused for that day, and that excusal is complete; the order continues nothing after that day.
